newsitem.title: USA: FTC staff still undecided on Staples.
newsitem.headline: FTC staff still undecided on Staples.

text.p: The chief executive officer of Staples Inc. said Thursday that staff at the Federal Trade Comission had made no decision on whether to recommend blocking his office superstore's merger with Office Depot Inc.

Others familiar with the talks, not affiliated with the two office superstores, agreed mid-level staff at the FTC had asked hard questions about the effect of the merger but had reached no final conclusions.

"We have been told by the FTC administrative staff at several levels that no decision has been made by the staff" on whether to recommend a preliminary injunction to block the merger, Staples CEO Thomas Stemberg said in a telephone interview from company headquarters in Westborough, Mass.

Stemberg also said there has been no discussion with FTC staff on selling off any of Staples or Office Depot's office superstores in the United States. Staples has 473 such stores and Office Depot, based in Delray Beach, Fla., has 511.
"There have been absolutely no discussions about divestitures," he said. Sometimes the FTC requires divestitures as a condition of mergers.

Representatives of Staples and Office Depot will meet with representatives of the FTC in the near future to make their case that the merger should take place, although Stemberg would not say exactly when.

Such a meeting must take place soon if the FTC is to meet a deadline of Feb. 25, which is when Staples said it has been promised a government decision. Office Depot and Staples have set Feb. 27 for stockholders meetings to consider the merger, originally announced last September.

Under FTC procedures, staff will make a recommendation to the five FTC commissioners about whether the merger should proceed. The commissioners make the final decision on whether to clear the merger or seek an injunction to block it.
The decision will turn on the question of "market definition."

If the FTC decides Office Depot and Staples are in a special market category of "office supply superstores," then their merger would leave OfficeMax Inc. as the only competitor. Narrowing the market from three to two superstores would likely run into trouble.
Staples argues that it is actually part of a huge market for office products that together with Office Depot has only a small share of the market.

Staples cites data from independent observers showing the two stores combined have shares on products like copy paper, writing instruments, inkjet cartridges, computer paper and toner that vary from as little as 4.5 percent up to roughly 16 percent.

Stemberg said the companies' joint business plan "foresees several billion dollars of cost savings between now and the year 2000" if the merger goes through and "the majority of these savings will be passed on to our customers" in the form of lower prices.

There have been reports that the FTC staff had alerted commissioners to the "possiblity" they would recommend a preliminary injunction blocking the merger. But such a possibility always exists as a decision draws near on a major merger, those familiar with FTC procedures said.
